The city that shares a border with the city where a person went to work during the gold rush in the biggest state in the USA by population is **Placerville**.

Here is the breakdown:
1.  **Biggest state by population:** California.
2.  **Gold rush city:** The most famous city associated with the start of the California Gold Rush (1848) is **Coloma**, where James W. Marshall discovered gold at Sutter's Mill. James Marshall himself worked there as a sawmill foreman for John Sutter.
3.  **Bordering city:** Coloma is located just south of **Placerville** (in the same county, El Dorado), and Placerville is widely recognized as the nearest city and historically served as the primary supply hub for the gold miners working in Coloma and the surrounding areas. While they are close neighbors separated by the American River and some distance, Placerville is the major city immediately adjacent to Coloma. Some sources describe them as being in close proximity or part of the same functional area ("Lotus and Coloma" is often listed as a neighborhood of Placerville in modern contexts, though historically they were distinct settlements).

However, it's worth noting that "going to work" could refer to anyone who went to the gold rush, but the specific location "where a person went to work" implies the site of employment or discovery, which is definitively Coloma. The city sharing a border with Coloma is Placerville.

Answer: **Placerville**

The **California gold rush** (1848–1855) was a gold rush in California, which began on January 24, 1848, when gold was found by James W. Marshall at [Sutter's Mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutter's_Mill "Sutter's Mill") in Coloma, California.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-1) The news of gold brought approximately 300,000 people from the rest of the United States and abroad to California, which had recently been conquered from Mexico. The sudden influx of gold into the money supply reinvigorated the American economy; the sudden population increase allowed California to grow rapidly into statehood in the Compromise of 1850. The gold rush had severe effects on Native Californians and accelerated the Native American population's decline from factors including disease, starvation, and according to certain sources, acts of unprovoked aggression.

The effects of the gold rush were substantial. The arrival of large numbers of "forty-niners" (referring to 1849, the peak year for gold rush immigration) led to significant conflict between the newcomers and indigenous people, eventually resulting in whole tribes being displaced in some cases. Outside of California, the first to arrive were from Oregon, Hawaii, and Latin America in late 1848. Of the approximately 300,000 people who came to California during the gold rush, about half arrived by sea and half came overland on the California Trail and the California Road; forty-niners often faced substantial hardships on the trip. While most of the newly arrived were Americans, the gold rush attracted thousands from Latin America, Europe, Australia, and China. Agriculture and ranching expanded throughout the state to meet the needs of the settlers. San Francisco grew from a small settlement of about 200 residents in 1846 to a boomtown of about 36,000 by 1852. Roads, churches, schools and other towns were built throughout California. In 1849, a state constitution was written. The new constitution was adopted by referendum vote; the future state's interim first governor and legislature were chosen. In September 1850, California achieved statehood.
At the beginning of the gold rush, there was no law regarding property rights in the goldfields and a system of "staking claims" was developed. Prospectors retrieved the gold from streams and riverbeds using simple techniques, such as panning. Although mining caused environmental harm, more sophisticated methods of gold recovery were developed and later adopted around the world. New methods of transportation developed as steamships came into regular service. By 1869, railroads were built from California to the eastern United States. At its peak, technological advances reached a point where significant financing was required, increasing the proportion of gold companies to individual miners. Gold worth tens of billions of today's US dollars was recovered, which led to great wealth for a few, though many who participated in the California gold rush earned little more than they had started with.

## History
### Earlier discoveries
Gold was discovered in California as early as March 9, 1842, at Rancho San Francisco, in the mountains north of present-day Los Angeles. Californian native Francisco Lopez was searching for stray horses and stopped on the bank of a small creek (in today's Placerita Canyon), about 3 miles (4.8 km) east of present-day Newhall, and about 35 miles (56 km) northwest of Los Angeles. While the horses grazed, Lopez dug up some wild onions and found a small gold nugget in the roots among the bulbs. He looked further and found more gold.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-blakely-2) Lopez took the gold to authorities who confirmed its worth. Lopez and others began to search for other streambeds with gold deposits in the area. They found several in the northeastern section of the forest, within present-day Ventura County.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-blakely-2) In November, some of the gold was sent to the U.S. Mint, but otherwise attracted little notice.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-RawlsPlacerita-4) In 1843, Lopez found gold in San Feliciano Canyon near his first discovery. Mexican miners from Sonora worked the placer deposits until 1846.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-blakely-2) Minor finds of gold in California were also made by Mission Indians prior to 1848. The friars instructed them to keep its location secret to avoid a gold rush.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-FOOTNOTERolle1987164-5)

## History
### Marshall's discovery
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Capt._Sutter's_account_of_the_first_discovery_of_the_Gold_Crop_Edit.jpg)

In January 1847, nine months into the Mexican–American War, the Treaty of Cahuenga was signed, leading to the resolution of the military conflict in Alta California (Upper California).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-6) On January 24, 1848, James W. Marshall[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-8) found shiny metal in the tailrace of a lumber mill he was building for Sacramento pioneer John Sutter—known as [Sutter's Mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutter's_Mill "Sutter's Mill"), near Coloma on the American River.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-BancroftDiscovery-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-CAMap-11) Marshall brought what he found to Sutter, and the two privately tested the metal. After the tests showed that it was gold, Sutter expressed dismay, wanting to keep the news quiet because he feared what would happen to his plans for an agricultural empire if there were a gold rush in the region.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-12) The Mexican–American War ended on May 30 with the ratification of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which formally transferred California to the United States.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-13)

## History
### Marshall's discovery
Having sworn all concerned at the mill to secrecy, in February 1848, Sutter sent Charles Bennett to Monterey to meet with Colonel Mason, the chief U.S. official in California, to secure the mineral rights of the land where the mill stood. Bennett was not to tell anyone of the discovery of gold, but when he stopped at Benicia, he heard talk about the discovery of coal near Mount Diablo, and he blurted out the discovery of gold. He continued to San Francisco, where again, he could not keep the secret. At Monterey, Mason declined to make any judgement of title to lands and mineral rights, and Bennett for the third time revealed the gold discovery.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBancroft1888[httpsarchiveorgdetailsbancrohistofcali23huberichpage42mode2up_42%E2%80%9344]-14)
By March 1848, rumors of the discovery were confirmed by San Francisco newspaper publisher and merchant Samuel Brannan. Brannan hurriedly set up a store to sell gold prospecting supplies,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-HollBran-15) and he walked through the streets of San Francisco, holding aloft a vial of gold, shouting "Gold! Gold! Gold from the American River!"[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBancroft1888[httpsarchiveorgdetailsbancrohistofcali23huberichpage55mode2up_55%E2%80%9356]-16)

## History
### Marshall's discovery
On August 19, 1848, _The New York Herald_ was the first major newspaper on the East Coast to report the discovery of gold. On December 5, 1848, US president James K. Polk confirmed the discovery of gold in an address to Congress.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-StarrCongress-17) As a result, individuals seeking to benefit from the gold rush—later called the "forty-niners"—began moving to the Gold Country of California or "Mother Lode" from other countries and from other parts of the United States. As Sutter had feared, his business plans were ruined after his workers left in search of gold, and squatters took over his land and stole his crops and cattle.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBancroft1888[httpsarchiveorgdetailsbancrohistofcali23huberichpage103mode2up_103%E2%80%93105]-18)

## History
### Marshall's discovery
San Francisco had been a tiny settlement before the rush began. When residents learned about the discovery, it at first became a ghost town of abandoned ships and businesses,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBancroft1888[httpsarchiveorgdetailsbancrohistofcali23huberichpage59mode2up_59%E2%80%9360]-19) but then boomed as merchants and new people arrived. The population of San Francisco increased quickly from about 1,000[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-HollidaySF-20) in 1848 to 25,000 full-time residents by 1850.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-RawlsSF-21) Miners lived in tents, wood shanties, or deck cabins removed from abandoned ships.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-HollInfra-22) There were no churches or religious services in the rapidly growing city, which prompted missionaries like William Taylor to meet the need, where he held services in the street, using a barrel head as his pulpit. Crowds would gather to listen to his sermons, and before long he received enough generous donations from successful gold miners and built San Francisco's first church.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_gold_rush#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor1895195-23)

Title: California Gold Rush drove mass migration, boom and upheaval

June 29, 2026, 8:00 a.m. ET
He picked up a pebble from the riverbed, set it on a rock and struck it with another.
The metal flattened instead of shattering.
In that moment on Jan. 24, 1848, James W. Marshall knew what he was holding.
Gold.
Within minutes, the carpenter and sawmill foreman gathered more glittering flakes along the American River, filling his hat with what he later estimated was about $15 worth — modest even then, but enough to change everything. The men working beside him, earning $1 a day and meals, quickly walked off the job to search for their own fortunes.
Marshall’s discovery at Sutter’s Mill set off the California Gold Rush — a turning point not just for the West, but for a young nation still defining its identity. As the United States approaches its 250th anniversary in 2026, the gold rush stands as one of the earliest and most consequential tests of the American promise: opportunity, mobility — and its costs.

## A discovery that reshaped a nation
The timing was pivotal.
Days after Marshall’s find, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the Mexican-American War and transferred California to U.S. control. What followed was one of the largest mass migrations in American history.
In 1848, California’s non-Native population was about 14,000. Within four years, it had surged to roughly 250,000. The so-called forty-niners came by land and sea — some crossing the continent by wagon over months, others sailing around Cape Horn or cutting through Panama.
San Francisco was transformed almost overnight, from a quiet port into a chaotic boomtown packed with tents, saloons, stores and speculation. Sacramento became a critical supply hub. New communities rose just as quickly as fortunes were made and lost.
At its peak in 1852, miners pulled tens of millions of dollars in gold from California’s rivers and hills — wealth that fueled banks, railroads and businesses nationwide.
“The economy just exploded,” said Ed Allen, a historian at Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park.

## The reality behind the rush
For most who came, the promise of instant wealth proved elusive.
Only a small percentage of miners struck it rich. Many spent what little they found just as quickly — a pattern fueled by scarcity, isolation and the cost of supplies. Some of the most reliable profits went not to miners, but to those who sold goods and services to them.
Companies such as Wells Fargo and Levi Strauss & Co. trace their roots to that era, providing banking, shipping and durable clothing built for the rough conditions of gold country.
The journey west itself was often more dangerous than the mining. Travelers faced disease, starvation and harsh terrain. Even after arrival, competition was fierce, claims were unstable, and violence was common.

## A boom built on displacement and discrimination
The gold rush also unleashed devastating consequences — particularly for California’s Native people.
Historians estimate the Native population in California fell dramatically during and after the rush, driven by disease, forced displacement, violence and state-sanctioned policies. By 1900, the number of Native Americans recorded in California had dropped to a fraction of its pre-contact population.
State and federal actions compounded the harm. In 1850, California imposed a Foreign Miners’ License Tax that targeted non-American miners — especially those from Mexico, Latin America, China and Europe — requiring them to pay steep monthly fees or abandon their claims.
Even after the tax was largely repealed, discrimination, exclusion and violence persisted, reshaping who could participate in the gold economy — and who could not.
For many historians, that legacy is inseparable from the narrative of growth.

## From pickaxes to processors
Nearly two centuries later, California remains a global magnet for those seeking opportunity — though the tools have changed.
Instead of pans and shovels, today’s seekers arrive with degrees, capital and code. Silicon Valley — home to companies such as Apple, Nvidia, Google and Meta — has become the center of another modern rush, driven by artificial intelligence and the promise of transformative wealth.
Like the miners of 1849, today’s innovators come from around the world, drawn by the possibility of building something new.
“The Gold Rush was this incredible moment of people converging in one place to pursue opportunity,” said Makeda Best of the Oakland Museum of California. “You can see echoes of that today.”
Venture capital, startups and new technologies have created cycles of boom and bust, but the underlying draw remains the same: California as a proving ground for ambition.

## The American promise — and its price
The story of the gold rush is often told as a celebration of ingenuity and risk-taking — qualities still central to the American identity.
But as the country marks 250 years since its founding, the legacy is more complicated.
The same forces that built fortunes also deepened inequality, accelerated environmental damage and led to violence and exclusion that reshaped entire communities.
That dual legacy — opportunity paired with consequence — continues to define California and the nation today.
The search for gold never really ended.
It just changed form.

He picked up a pebble from the riverbed, set it on a rock and struck it with another.
The metal flattened instead of shattering.
In that moment on Jan. 24, 1848, James W. Marshall knew what he was holding.
Gold.
Within minutes, the carpenter and sawmill foreman gathered more glittering flakes along the American River, filling his hat with what he later estimated was about $15 worth — modest even then, but enough to change everything. The men working beside him, earning $1 a day and meals, quickly walked off the job to search for their own fortunes.
Marshall’s discovery at Sutter’s Mill set off the California Gold Rush — a turning point not just for the West, but for a young nation still defining its identity. As the United States approaches its 250th anniversary in 2026, the gold rush stands as one of the earliest and most consequential tests of the American promise: opportunity, mobility — and its costs.

## A discovery that reshaped a nation
The timing was pivotal.
Days after Marshall’s find, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the Mexican-American War and transferred California to U.S. control. What followed was one of the largest mass migrations in American history.
In 1848, California’s non-Native population was about 14,000. Within four years, it had surged to roughly 250,000. The so-called forty-niners came by land and sea — some crossing the continent by wagon over months, others sailing around Cape Horn or cutting through Panama.
San Francisco was transformed almost overnight, from a quiet port into a chaotic boomtown packed with tents, saloons, stores and speculation. Sacramento became a critical supply hub. New communities rose just as quickly as fortunes were made and lost.
At its peak in 1852, miners pulled tens of millions of dollars in gold from California’s rivers and hills — wealth that fueled banks, railroads and businesses nationwide.
“The economy just exploded,” said Ed Allen, a historian at Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park.
texts.2:
## The reality behind the rush
For most who came, the promise of instant wealth proved elusive.
Only a small percentage of miners struck it rich. Many spent what little they found just as quickly — a pattern fueled by scarcity, isolation and the cost of supplies. Some of the most reliable profits went not to miners, but to those who sold goods and services to them.
Companies such as Wells Fargo and Levi Strauss & Co. trace their roots to that era, providing banking, shipping and durable clothing built for the rough conditions of gold country.
The journey west itself was often more dangerous than the mining. Travelers faced disease, starvation and harsh terrain. Even after arrival, competition was fierce, claims were unstable, and violence was common.
texts.3:
## A boom built on displacement and discrimination
The gold rush also unleashed devastating consequences — particularly for California’s Native people.
Historians estimate the Native population in California fell dramatically during and after the rush, driven by disease, forced displacement, violence and state-sanctioned policies. By 1900, the number of Native Americans recorded in California had dropped to a fraction of its pre-contact population.
State and federal actions compounded the harm. In 1850, California imposed a Foreign Miners’ License Tax that targeted non-American miners — especially those from Mexico, Latin America, China and Europe — requiring them to pay steep monthly fees or abandon their claims.
Even after the tax was largely repealed, discrimination, exclusion and violence persisted, reshaping who could participate in the gold economy — and who could not.
For many historians, that legacy is inseparable from the narrative of growth.
texts.4:
## From pickaxes to processors
Nearly two centuries later, California remains a global magnet for those seeking opportunity — though the tools have changed.
Instead of pans and shovels, today’s seekers arrive with degrees, capital and code. Silicon Valley — home to companies such as Apple, Nvidia, Google and Meta — has become the center of another modern rush, driven by artificial intelligence and the promise of transformative wealth.
Like the miners of 1849, today’s innovators come from around the world, drawn by the possibility of building something new.
“The Gold Rush was this incredible moment of people converging in one place to pursue opportunity,” said Makeda Best of the Oakland Museum of California. “You can see echoes of that today.”
Venture capital, startups and new technologies have created cycles of boom and bust, but the underlying draw remains the same: California as a proving ground for ambition.
texts.5:
## The American promise — and its price
The story of the gold rush is often told as a celebration of ingenuity and risk-taking — qualities still central to the American identity.
But as the country marks 250 years since its founding, the legacy is more complicated.
The same forces that built fortunes also deepened inequality, accelerated environmental damage and led to violence and exclusion that reshaped entire communities.
That dual legacy — opportunity paired with consequence — continues to define California and the nation today.
The search for gold never really ended.
It just changed form.

He picked up a pebble from the riverbed, set it on a rock and struck it with another.
The metal flattened instead of shattering.
In that moment on Jan. 24, 1848, James W. Marshall knew what he was holding.
Gold.
Within minutes, the carpenter and sawmill foreman gathered more glittering flakes along the American River, filling his hat with what he later estimated was about $15 worth — modest even then, but enough to change everything. The men working beside him, earning $1 a day and meals, quickly walked off the job to search for their own fortunes.
Marshall’s discovery at Sutter’s Mill set off the California Gold Rush — a turning point not just for the West, but for a young nation still defining its identity. As the United States approaches its 250th anniversary in 2026, the gold rush stands as one of the earliest and most consequential tests of the American promise: opportunity, mobility — and its costs.

## A discovery that reshaped a nation
The timing was pivotal.
Days after Marshall’s find, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the Mexican-American War and transferred California to U.S. control. What followed was one of the largest mass migrations in American history.
In 1848, California’s non-Native population was about 14,000. Within four years, it had surged to roughly 250,000. The so-called forty-niners came by land and sea — some crossing the continent by wagon over months, others sailing around Cape Horn or cutting through Panama.
San Francisco was transformed almost overnight, from a quiet port into a chaotic boomtown packed with tents, saloons, stores and speculation. Sacramento became a critical supply hub. New communities rose just as quickly as fortunes were made and lost.
At its peak in 1852, miners pulled tens of millions of dollars in gold from California’s rivers and hills — wealth that fueled banks, railroads and businesses nationwide.
“The economy just exploded,” said Ed Allen, a historian at Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park.

## The reality behind the rush
For most who came, the promise of instant wealth proved elusive.
Only a small percentage of miners struck it rich. Many spent what little they found just as quickly — a pattern fueled by scarcity, isolation and the cost of supplies. Some of the most reliable profits went not to miners, but to those who sold goods and services to them.
Companies such as Wells Fargo and Levi Strauss & Co. trace their roots to that era, providing banking, shipping and durable clothing built for the rough conditions of gold country.
The journey west itself was often more dangerous than the mining. Travelers faced disease, starvation and harsh terrain. Even after arrival, competition was fierce, claims were unstable, and violence was common.

## A boom built on displacement and discrimination
The gold rush also unleashed devastating consequences — particularly for California’s Native people.
Historians estimate the Native population in California fell dramatically during and after the rush, driven by disease, forced displacement, violence and state-sanctioned policies. By 1900, the number of Native Americans recorded in California had dropped to a fraction of its pre-contact population.
State and federal actions compounded the harm. In 1850, California imposed a Foreign Miners’ License Tax that targeted non-American miners — especially those from Mexico, Latin America, China and Europe — requiring them to pay steep monthly fees or abandon their claims.
Even after the tax was largely repealed, discrimination, exclusion and violence persisted, reshaping who could participate in the gold economy — and who could not.
For many historians, that legacy is inseparable from the narrative of growth.

## From pickaxes to processors
Nearly two centuries later, California remains a global magnet for those seeking opportunity — though the tools have changed.
Instead of pans and shovels, today’s seekers arrive with degrees, capital and code. Silicon Valley — home to companies such as Apple, Nvidia, Google and Meta — has become the center of another modern rush, driven by artificial intelligence and the promise of transformative wealth.
Like the miners of 1849, today’s innovators come from around the world, drawn by the possibility of building something new.
“The Gold Rush was this incredible moment of people converging in one place to pursue opportunity,” said Makeda Best of the Oakland Museum of California. “You can see echoes of that today.”
Venture capital, startups and new technologies have created cycles of boom and bust, but the underlying draw remains the same: California as a proving ground for ambition.

## The American promise — and its price
The story of the gold rush is often told as a celebration of ingenuity and risk-taking — qualities still central to the American identity.
But as the country marks 250 years since its founding, the legacy is more complicated.
The same forces that built fortunes also deepened inequality, accelerated environmental damage and led to violence and exclusion that reshaped entire communities.
That dual legacy — opportunity paired with consequence — continues to define California and the nation today.
The search for gold never really ended.
It just changed form.

**Coloma** (Nisenan: _Cullumah_, meaning "beautiful") is a census-designated place (CDP)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-6) in El Dorado County, California, United States. It is approximately 36 miles (58 km) northeast of Sacramento. Coloma is most noted for being the site where James W. Marshall found gold in the Sierra Nevada foothills, at [Sutter's Mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutter's_Mill "Sutter's Mill") on January 24, 1848,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-nrhpinv2-3) leading to the California gold rush. As of the 2020 census, Coloma had a population of 521.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-Census2020PLLede-7)
The settlement is a tourist attraction known for its ghost town and the centerpiece of the Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park. Coloma was designated a National Historic Landmark District on July 4, 1961.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-nrhpinv2-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-nhlsum-5)
Coloma lies at an elevation of 764 feet (233 m).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-gnis-2)

The name comes from the Nisenan Native Americans name for the valley in which Coloma is located: _Cullumah_, meaning 'beautiful.' Coloma is on the South Fork American River that runs through the valley and was built on the original Indian village of Koloma.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-8) Former spellings include "Colluma" and "Culloma".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-CGN-9)
Coloma grew around Sutter's Mill following the finding of gold. A post office was established in 1849 under the name Culloma, changing to Coloma in 1851.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-CGN-9)
One of Coloma's earliest settlers was Silas Sanderson (1824–1886), who went on to become the 7th Chief Justice of California.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-10) Another was Nancy Gooch, who was one of the first black women to succeed in California.
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ROBERT_BELL'S_STORE,_COLOMA,_CALIFORNIA.jpg)
Robert Bell's store in Coloma
While some people still live in the area, Coloma is considered something of a ghost town because civic buildings such as the jail have been abandoned and left to decay, and other buildings from its boom era (1847–1852) have been converted into museums and other historical displays. The tailrace of Sutter's Mill remains, as does a nearby reconstruction.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-marshall-11)
In reality the meaningfulness of the township of Coloma has dissipated as residents who live in the wider Coloma Valley area generally share a community spirit.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-12)

The local economy is based predominantly on agriculture[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-13) and tourism. Of particular note is the rafting industry as the South Fork American River is one of the most popular white-water trips in North America.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-14)

**Coloma** (Nisenan: _Cullumah_, meaning "beautiful") is a census-designated place (CDP)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-6) in El Dorado County, California, United States. It is approximately 36 miles (58 km) northeast of Sacramento. Coloma is most noted for being the site where James W. Marshall found gold in the Sierra Nevada foothills, at [Sutter's Mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutter's_Mill "Sutter's Mill") on January 24, 1848,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-nrhpinv2-3) leading to the California gold rush. As of the 2020 census, Coloma had a population of 521.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-Census2020PLLede-7)
The settlement is a tourist attraction known for its ghost town and the centerpiece of the Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park. Coloma was designated a National Historic Landmark District on July 4, 1961.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-nrhpinv2-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-nhlsum-5)
Coloma lies at an elevation of 764 feet (233 m).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-gnis-2)
texts.2:
The name comes from the Nisenan Native Americans name for the valley in which Coloma is located: _Cullumah_, meaning 'beautiful.' Coloma is on the South Fork American River that runs through the valley and was built on the original Indian village of Koloma.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-8) Former spellings include "Colluma" and "Culloma".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-CGN-9)
Coloma grew around Sutter's Mill following the finding of gold. A post office was established in 1849 under the name Culloma, changing to Coloma in 1851.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-CGN-9)
One of Coloma's earliest settlers was Silas Sanderson (1824–1886), who went on to become the 7th Chief Justice of California.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-10) Another was Nancy Gooch, who was one of the first black women to succeed in California.
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ROBERT_BELL'S_STORE,_COLOMA,_CALIFORNIA.jpg)
Robert Bell's store in Coloma
While some people still live in the area, Coloma is considered something of a ghost town because civic buildings such as the jail have been abandoned and left to decay, and other buildings from its boom era (1847–1852) have been converted into museums and other historical displays. The tailrace of Sutter's Mill remains, as does a nearby reconstruction.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-marshall-11)
In reality the meaningfulness of the township of Coloma has dissipated as residents who live in the wider Coloma Valley area generally share a community spirit.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-12)
texts.3:
The local economy is based predominantly on agriculture[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-13) and tourism. Of particular note is the rafting industry as the South Fork American River is one of the most popular white-water trips in North America.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-14)

**Coloma** (Nisenan: _Cullumah_, meaning "beautiful") is a census-designated place (CDP)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-6) in El Dorado County, California, United States. It is approximately 36 miles (58 km) northeast of Sacramento. Coloma is most noted for being the site where James W. Marshall found gold in the Sierra Nevada foothills, at [Sutter's Mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutter's_Mill "Sutter's Mill") on January 24, 1848,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-nrhpinv2-3) leading to the California gold rush. As of the 2020 census, Coloma had a population of 521.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-Census2020PLLede-7)
The settlement is a tourist attraction known for its ghost town and the centerpiece of the Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park. Coloma was designated a National Historic Landmark District on July 4, 1961.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-nrhpinv2-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-nhlsum-5)
Coloma lies at an elevation of 764 feet (233 m).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-gnis-2)

The name comes from the Nisenan Native Americans name for the valley in which Coloma is located: _Cullumah_, meaning 'beautiful.' Coloma is on the South Fork American River that runs through the valley and was built on the original Indian village of Koloma.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-8) Former spellings include "Colluma" and "Culloma".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-CGN-9)
Coloma grew around Sutter's Mill following the finding of gold. A post office was established in 1849 under the name Culloma, changing to Coloma in 1851.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-CGN-9)
One of Coloma's earliest settlers was Silas Sanderson (1824–1886), who went on to become the 7th Chief Justice of California.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-10) Another was Nancy Gooch, who was one of the first black women to succeed in California.
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ROBERT_BELL'S_STORE,_COLOMA,_CALIFORNIA.jpg)
Robert Bell's store in Coloma
While some people still live in the area, Coloma is considered something of a ghost town because civic buildings such as the jail have been abandoned and left to decay, and other buildings from its boom era (1847–1852) have been converted into museums and other historical displays. The tailrace of Sutter's Mill remains, as does a nearby reconstruction.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-marshall-11)
In reality the meaningfulness of the township of Coloma has dissipated as residents who live in the wider Coloma Valley area generally share a community spirit.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-12)

The local economy is based predominantly on agriculture[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-13) and tourism. Of particular note is the rafting industry as the South Fork American River is one of the most popular white-water trips in North America.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-14)
